A1.justification: Both PDFs describe NSF-SCIFY with the same authors, extraction approach, and retained materials-science experiments. The main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset analyses, abstract classification experiments, and fine-tuning results for three tasks in Tables 2–4.

after.justification: v3 retains those original results and adds cross-directorate experiments, extraction-quality evaluations, taxonomy analyses, and error analyses.

M1.justification: Both versions use joint zero-shot extraction with Claude-3.5, LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral and Qwen, and GPT-4o-mini pairwise evaluation. Renaming verifiable_claims to claims preserves its definition. Applying the approach to NSF-SCIFY-20K and proposing future remedies do not establish a changed extraction or training method.

E1.justification: v1's downstream experiments use the materials-science subset. v3 additionally trains and evaluates on NSF-SCIFY-20K, spanning MPS, GEO, ENG, CSE, and BIO, and evaluates extraction quality across six areas by separating materials science from the rest of MPS. This substantially broadens the empirically studied domains while retaining the three tasks.

E2.justification: The Mistral and Qwen comparisons in Tables 2–4 remain unchanged. Section 7 and Appendix I newly use Claude-extracted claims as a comparison in the error analysis of fine-tuned Mistral outputs; Claude previously served as the dataset generator without this reported error comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds a validation protocol sampling 20 awards from each of six areas, using GPT-4o to identify missing or incorrect extractions and manually checking its outputs on 20 abstracts. It also reports pairwise-judge validation and a separate 120-award error-analysis sample. These substantially extend evaluation design; the original materials-science split, preprocessing, training budget, and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds claim and proposal taxonomies, extraction precision/recall analyses across scientific areas, human-assisted judge validation, a reported evaluation-prompt robustness check, and detailed error categories with examples in Appendix I. v1's abstract-style analysis and qualitative joint-versus-separate extraction observation are retained.

E5.justification: v1 already reports 95% confidence-interval ranges for Tables 2–4, which v3 retains. v3 additionally specifies standard-deviation error bars from 1,000 bootstrap resamples in Figures 5–6. Appendix F displays per-score uncertainties without clearly identifying their interpretation. No increase in training runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: Tables 2–4 retain their numerical results. New NSF-SCIFY-20K results in Tables A5–A7 include base versus fine-tuned Mistral claim F-scores of 0.5247 versus 0.7268, alongside lower recall of 0.8141 versus 0.7354. v3 also adds domain-specific extraction-quality results, taxonomy distributions, and error rates. These are additional results under new coverage, rather than improvements over v1 under identical conditions.

T1.justification: The pairwise support functions and mathematical precision/recall definitions are retained. The new true-positive, false-positive, and false-negative description explains standard evaluation quantities; neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that change.

C1.justification: v1 describes the full 2.8-million-claim corpus as an estimate awaiting comprehensive processing. v3 presents that size without the estimate qualification, adds NSF-SCIFY-20K as an explicit contribution, and foregrounds high-precision extraction with lower recall. This materially strengthens and broadens the dataset contribution while retaining the three-task and fine-tuning claims.

C2.justification: v3 introduces substantial limitations concerning funded-US-proposal coverage, availability bias, older publication links, generalizability, limited baselines, and LLM evaluation validity. It interprets lower claim recall as a deliberate precision-first choice and discusses error mechanisms and possible remedies. These qualifications go substantially beyond v1's advantages and brief future-work discussion.

D1.justification: v3 adds explicit code and checkpoint locations, stated Apache-2.0 release terms in Appendix A, and approximately one hour of training per epoch. Much of the release description and the extraction/evaluation prompts already existed and is relocated. The PDFs establish improved access documentation, not independently verified resource availability.

R1.justification: v3 adds Gu et al.'s LLM-as-judge survey, Liu et al.'s G-Eval, and GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini references, and explicitly connects its claim definition to the already-cited Tang et al. The principal related-work comparison and grant-abstract novelty positioning remain largely unchanged; publication updates to existing references are bibliographic changes.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the abstract, expands short task descriptions into explanatory paragraphs, substantially recasts the conclusion, and reorganizes the narrative around dataset validation, error analysis, and structured limitations. The appendices are reorganized to include reproducibility and separate analyses, with existing prompts and release material moved.

P2.justification: v3 adds two taxonomy treemaps, two extraction-quality plots, three results tables, two taxonomy-example tables, and formatted error-example panels. The original t-SNE figure moves to Appendix E as Figure A7, and existing example tables become A8–A9. Table 1 gains a subset row, and numerous captions gain emphasized summaries.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens a dataset paper whose earlier validation centered on materials-science downstream scores and qualitative extraction checks. Cross-directorate experiments, sampled extraction-quality and judge validation, and error analyses provide important evidence about reliability and incomplete coverage; explicit limitations improve interpretation. These gains outweigh weaknesses in the additions: human agreement remains described only as near-perfect, and the proposal taxonomy says eight categories in Section 4.2 but lists ten in Table A11, with some mismatched examples.
